chunks: Why inductor current is a linear ramp. The question: Why is the inductor current a linear ramp? What determines this behavior?
The inductor current in a buck is a straight-line ramp because the voltage across the inductor is nearly constant.
The inductor's rule is that voltage equals inductance times how fast the current changes. A steady voltage therefore gives a steady rate of change, which is a straight line.
Think of a car under constant acceleration. The speed climbs in a straight line, not a curve.
The voltage across the inductor is like the push, and the inductance is like the weight of the car: a heavier car (bigger L ) gains speed more slowly.
The straight line holds only while the push stays constant.
The inductor voltage in CCM is a two-level rectangle. Because it is constant on each segment, the current slope is constant on each segment.
Inductance ( L ): how strongly the coil resists changes in current, in henries ("Inductor differential equation"). di over dt : how fast the current is changing, its slope.
Inductor voltage: the voltage across the coil, which sets the slope. Ripple: the small up-and-down swing of the current around its average.
Saturation: when the core can't store more and the inductance collapses.
Use 10 volts in, 5 volts out, 10 microhenries and a 2 microseconds cycle at 50 percent duty.
While the switch is on, the inductor sees 10 minus 5 equals 5 volts, so the current rises at 5 over 10 equals 0. 5 amps per µs. After 1 microseconds it has risen 0. 5 amps.
While off, it sees 5 volts the other way and falls at the same rate for 1 microseconds. That is the whole idea.
"It follows from v equals L di over dt . In the on state the inductor sees roughly V in-V out , constant, so the current rises linearly with slope (V in-V out) over L .
In the off state it sees -V out , constant, so it falls linearly at V out over L .
The slope depends only on those voltages and L , not on the load; the load just sets the average of the triangle.
It's only approximately linear, assuming small ripple and negligible resistive drops, and it breaks if the inductor saturates."
